This issue is discussed in source [7], which points out that the time scales for structural deformation modes are generally much less than the time scales for pressure decrease for nuclear weapons pressure pulses. For this reason, use of the peak value as the threshold for failure is appropriate for approximating the effect of nuclear sources. For smaller explosive charges nearby pipelines, the time scale of the pressure pulse is much closer to the time scale of structural collapse, and thus the dynamics of the problem need to be considered. 3.3. Effect of Parameter Variation The equations provide insight into how variation of parameters affects collapse pressures. Inspection of the terms in the expressions and numerical experiments indicate that:  Internal pressurization can have a large effect on pressure needed for failure. Expected pressures vary from 100 to 1500 psi. In general, this pressure must be exceeded by the external loading to start on the path toward cross-sectional yielding or buckling, so can increase the needed pressure by a factor of two to three. It has minimal effect on longitudinal collapse, however.  Depth of burial can affect collapse pressure. Numerical experimentation has shown that a 4x increase in burial depth increases the required pressure for collapse by a factor of 2.  Out-of-roundness has a very strong effect on pressure required for collapse. The first equation for cross-sectional buckling shows an order-of-magnitude reduction in pressure for collapse when the initial deflection starts at 8% instead of 0.1% as assumed here. Realistic estimates of typical in-situ deflection would be very helpful in guiding how important this is in practice. 14 4. CONCLUSIONS This report identifies a set of expressions from pipeline design literature that describe the pressure- driven collapse of pipelines. The expressions concern three failure mechanisms: cross-sectional yielding, cross-sectional buckling, and longitudinal buckling. Expressions for cross-sectional buckling have different forms for above- and below-ground pipes. These expressions are then applied to a set of representative pipelines relevant for natural gas distribution networks, which provide estimates on the needed overpressures and dynamic pressures for pipeline failure. Pressures from a set of nuclear source terms provide means to assess distance from ground zero within which pipelines would collapse. The expressions provide a first approximation to pipeline damage useful for inclusion within rapid-turnaround scenario assessment tools. 15 16 REFERENCES [1] Stephenson, D.
